title: The Day Steam Power Changed The World
fullText: Think about the last time you boiled water for coffee. You filled the kettle, clicked a button, and walked away. 30 seconds later, steam was curling off the surface like it meant nothing. It didn't used to mean nothing. That same steam, that same physics, that same angry pressurized [music] energy once tore apart iron boilers and killed dozens in a single afternoon. It drove ships across oceans without a single sail. It pulled 100 ton loads of coal up from half a mile underground. It connected an entire continent with iron rails [music] and it did all of it in less than a 100red years. Before steam, the world moved at the speed of a horse. After steam, it moved at a speed no one had words for yet. This is the story of how a broken machine, a Scottish instrument maker, and one very cold walk through a park in Glasgow rewired civilization from the ground up. To understand what steam power actually did, you have to understand just how exhausting the world was before it existed. Everything heavy that needed moving was moved by muscle. Human muscle, animal muscle. If you needed to grind grain, [music] you hitched a horse to a mill. If you needed to pump water, you put a man on a lever and he pumped until his arms gave out. If you needed to cross the Atlantic, you waited for the wind and then you waited some more. The fastest thing on Earth was a galloping horse about 30 mph [music] and only for a few minutes before it collapsed. Life was local in a way that's almost impossible to imagine now. Most people in 18th century England lived and died within [music] 20 mi of where they were born. Not because they didn't want to travel, because travel was brutal, expensive, and slow. A coach from London to Edinburgh took 4 days in good weather. In bad weather, it might not make it at all. And none of that was the real problem. [music] The real problem was coal. England in the early 1700s had a crisis that was quietly strangling the entire economy. The country had burned through most of its surface timber. Wood, the fuel that had powered England for centuries, was running [music] out. Coal was the obvious replacement. England had enormous coal deposits, particularly in the north and in Wales. But here was the catch. The easy coal was already gone. To get to the coal that remained, miners had to go deeper. And the deeper they went, the more water seeped in. Natural groundwater, underground springs, rain filtering down through rock. The mines flooded [music] constantly. Workers spent half their shifts not mining coal, but bailing water out by hand or operating hand pumps in the dark. Some mines had to be abandoned entirely, not because the coal ran out, but because nobody could keep up with the water. The richest [music] country in the world with some of the largest coal reserves on the planet was slowly drowning in its own mines. That was the problem someone needed to solve. And the first people who tried to solve it nearly blew themselves up. The first steam powered device ever put [music] to practical use was called the miner's friend. That name was either very optimistic or deeply ironic depending on how you look at it. Thomas Savory was an English military engineer who patented his machine in 1698. The concept was straightforward. Heat water into steam. Use the pressure of that steam [music] to push water upward out of a mine. When the steam cools and condenses, it creates a vacuum that sucks more water up behind it. On paper, it worked. In practice, it was a disaster. The pressures involved were far beyond what anyone [music] fully understood at the time. Savory's boilers cracked. They leaked. In at least several documented cases, [music] they exploded. And even when they worked, they could only lift water about 30 ft. Nowhere near enough for the deep mines that needed help most. The miner's friend turned out to be nobody's friend, but it pointed the way. 14 years later, a Devon ironmonger named [music] Thomas Newman built something genuinely better. His atmospheric engine, first installed in 1712 at a coal mine in Staferture, was the first machine that could actually do sustained useful work powered by steam. It was also enormous, slow, and staggeringly inefficient. Here is how it worked. Steam from a boiler rose into a large cylinder. Cold water was then injected into the cylinder, cooling the steam and causing it to condense. That condensation created a partial vacuum. Atmospheric pressure from outside the cylinder pushed a piston down into that vacuum. That piston was connected by a beam to a pump. Down goes the piston. Up comes the water. It worked. Mines that had been written off as unfixable were being drained within a few years. By 1730, dozens of newcomer engines were running across England. But the machine had a fundamental flaw that nobody seemed able to crack. Every single stroke of that piston required the entire cylinder to be cooled down with cold water and then heated back up again with fresh steam. Heat it, cool it, heat it, cool it over and over, thousands of times a day. The cylinder was the most expensive part of the engine to operate, and it was spending most of its energy doing nothing useful, just absorbing heat, then throwing it away. A new Kman engine burned enormous quantities of coal to do its job. It was just barely efficient enough to make economic [music] sense when it sat directly next to a coal mine, burning the cheapest possible fuel. Move it anywhere else, and the fuel costs [music] would eat you alive. The engine that saved the English coal industry couldn't be powered by anything except coal. It was progress, but it was a trap. For half a century, nobody found a way out of it. And then a young man in Glasgow was handed a broken newcomer model and told to fix it. James Watt was not a grand figure when he arrived at the University of Glasgow in 1757. He was 21 years old, the son of a Scottish merchant and ships Chandler. And he had come to the university not as a student but as a craftsman. His job was to repair and maintain the scientific instruments that the professors used in their lectures. Quadrants, scales, compasses, and [music] measuring devices of every kind. He was good at it. Quietly, methodically good in the way that some people are good at understanding how things fit together. In the winter of 1763, a professor named John Anderson handed him a small working model of a new Kman atmospheric engine. It had been sent to London for repairs, comeback still [music] broken, and now nobody knew what to do with it. What took it apart? He got it running within a few weeks. But as he watched it work, he became preoccupied with [music] something that had nothing to do with the repair job. The model was consuming an absurd amount of steam [music] relative to its tiny size, far more than the math said it should need. He started measuring. He started calculating. The problem, he realized, was [music] exactly what engineers had been quietly aware of, but unable to solve for 50 years. The cylinder, heating it, cooling [music] it, heating it again. enormous amounts of thermal energy just being thrown away with every single stroke. Watts spent months on the problem. He filled notebooks with calculations. He tested different designs, different materials, different sequences. Nothing worked. And then on a Sunday in May of 1765, he went for a walk. The specific location was Glasgow Green, a public park on the eastern edge of the city. It was a place Watt apparently walked often when he needed to think. He was turning the cylinder problem over in his mind when the answer arrived. Not gradually, but all at once. The reason the cylinder had to be cooled was to condense the steam. The reason the cylinder had to be reheated was to accept [music] new steam on the next stroke. What if those two things didn't have to happen in the same place? What if you kept the cylinder hot all the [music] time and piped the spent steam into a separate permanently cold vessel, a separate condenser where it would condense without ever cooling the cylinder itself. The cylinder stays hot. The condenser stays cold. The engine runs continuously without wasting energy, reheating its own [music] guts with every stroke. He later said the idea came to him before he had walked as far as the golf house. It took him another 11 years to turn that idea into a commercially viable engine. That gap between the moment of insight and [music] the moment it actually changed anything is one of the most important parts of this story and also one of the most overlooked. The money ran out multiple [music] times. Watt took on surveying work, designing canals and harbors [music] across Scotland just to keep himself financially alive while he kept developing the engine in whatever spare time [music] he had. He formed a partnership with John Robuk, an industrialist who agreed to fund [music] the work in exchange for a share of future profits. Robuk then went bankrupt in 1772, taking much of what Watt had built with him. The patent Watt [music] had filed in 1769 was ticking down. Patents in 18th century England re ran for 14 years. By the time Watt emerged from bankruptcy proceedings [music] and found a new partner, more than half that window was already gone. The new partner was Matthew Bolton, a Birmingham manufacturer who ran a large metalwork [music] factory called the Soho Manufactury. Bolton was one of the more remarkable businessmen of his era, not because he had capital, [music] which he did, but because he understood immediately what what had built. He reportedly said with the particular confidence of [music] someone who already knows he's right. I sell here, sir, what all the [music] world desires to have, power. Bolton lobbyed Parliament to extend Watts patent. He got it extended by 25 years. He threw the full resources of the Soho manufactury behind the engine. And in 1776, the same year the American colonies declared their independence from Britain, the first commercial Bolton and Watt engine was installed [music] and running. The cylinder stayed hot. The condenser stayed cold. The engine used roughly 3/4 less coal than a new Kman machine of equivalent power. If you're finding this story as fascinating as I do, go ahead and [clears throat] hit subscribe. History [music] like this, the moments where everything quietly pivots, is exactly what this channel [music] covers every week. Now, back to 1776 because things are about to move very fast. The first Bolton and Watt engines were still just fancy pumps. Extremely efficient, increasingly reliable fancy pumps, but pumps. They moved up and down. They drained mines. They didn't go anywhere. It was Watt himself who changed that. In 1781, he patented a mechanism called the sun and planet gear, which converted the up and down motion of a piston into [music] continuous rotational motion. A spinning shaft. And a spinning shaft could be connected [music] to almost anything. Within 5 years, Bolton and Watt engines were running cotton mills in Manchester. flower mills in London, breweries, iron foundaries, anywhere that previously required water wheels or horsepowered mills. A steam engine could now do the same job better, faster, without needing to be built next to a river and without stopping when the water level dropped in a dry summer. The textile industry, which had been the single largest employer in England for generations, transformed almost overnight. A skilled handw weaver in 1780 could produce a certain amount of cloth per day. By 1800, a steam powered loom operated by a largely unskilled worker could produce many times that amount at a fraction of the cost. The economics of cloth production were shattered and rebuilt from scratch in less than a generation. But all of that was just a warm-up for what came next. In 1804, a Cornish engineer named Richard Trevik strapped a steam engine to a set of iron rails and created something that had never existed in human history, a self-propelled vehicle. His locomotive hauled 10 tons of iron ore along a 5m stretch of track in southern Wales at a speed of approximately 5 mph. It wasn't fast. It wasn't reliable. The locomotive broke down several times during the journey, but the crowd that watched it that day understood they were seeing something that mattered. 25 years later, the question of what steam locomotion could actually become was answered definitively. In October of 1829, a public competition was held at Rainhill near Liverpool [music] to determine which locomotive would be chosen to power the newly constructed Liverpool and Manchester Railway. Five locomotives entered. One of them, built by a 48-year-old engineer named [music] George Stevenson and his son Robert, was called the Rocket. The rocket averaged 12 mph over the course of the trials. At its peak, [music] it hit 29 mph. Crowds watching from the trackside panicked. Newspaper reporters wrote that passengers would be unable to breathe at such velocities. A prominent physician warned publicly [music] that the human body could not survive sustained travel at speeds exceeding 20 mph that the rush of air would collapse the lungs. The rocket won the competition. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened the following year and the modern railroad era began. By 1850, there were more than 6,000 mi of railroad track in Britain. A country where two generations earlier, the journey of 200 m took 4 days by coach [music] could now be crossed in a matter of hours. In America, the transformation was even more dramatic because America had more space for it. The IAS transcontinental railroad completed in 1869 when the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines met at Promonary Summit Utah reduced the journey from the east coast to [music] California from 6 months by wagon or several weeks by sea to about a week by rail. A continent that had taken generations to cross was stitched together in roughly a decade of construction. The two golden spikes driven [music] at Promonary Summit on May 10th, 1869, a ceremonial gold spike and a silver spike [music] were connected to the telegraph lines alongside the tracks so that the hammer blows could be transmitted instantaneously [music] across the country. The moment they were struck, bells rang in San Francisco, in Chicago, in New York, and in Washington [music] DC simultaneously. That was the world steam had built, simultaneous, [music] connected, shocked by its own speed. But here is what tends to get left out of the triumphant version of this story. The steam-powered industrial revolution was not an unambiguous gift. For a very large number of people, particularly in its first several decades, it was something closer to a catastrophe. The factory system that steam made possible was built on labor conditions that would be unrecognizable today. Children as young as six worked [music] 12 to 14-hour shifts in textile mills small enough to crawl under the machinery to clear blockages, often losing fingers, sometimes their lives in [music] the process. Adults worked comparable hours for wages that kept [music] them permanently one bad week from destitution. The new industrial cities, Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, Pittsburgh, Lel [music] grew faster than any city in history had ever grown before. And they grew without sewers, without building codes, without any of the infrastructure that makes urban [music] life survivable. Housing was thrown up in days. Streets filled with waste. [music] Life expectancy in industrial Manchester in the 1840s was around 28 [music] years. That is not a typo. And then there were the boilers. Steam power [music] depended on containing enormous pressures inside iron vessels. When those vessels failed, and they failed [music] regularly because metallurgy was still being invented because inspection standards didn't exist because some operators pushed their equipment well past what it could handle. The results were catastrophic. Between 1816 [music] and 1848, there were more than 1,000 recorded steam boiler explosions in the United States alone. Entire riverboats simply ceased to exist. The Sultana disaster of 1865, the worst maritime disaster in American history, killed roughly 1,800 people when a poorly repaired boiler exploded [music] on the Mississippi River. Those numbers were slowly and unevenly the reason that safety regulations got invented. But they came after the deaths, not before. The craftsmen and [music] artisans who had spent their lives mastering hand trades found their skills rendered worthless by steampowered machinery. In a matter of years, the handloom weavers of Northern [music] England, who had worked as skilled, relatively well-paid independent craftsmen for generations were replaced by machine operators earning a fraction of what they had [music] made. Many of them ended up in the same mills where the machines that replaced them were running. Their [music] response was the lite movement of 1811 to 1816 in which groups of textile workers broke into mills at night and systematically destroyed the machinery. The word [music] lite has come to mean someone who blindly fears technology. That is not what the original lites were. They were skilled workers who understood exactly what was happening to them and who had no legal or political mechanism to stop it. framebreaking was made a capital offense in 1812. The British government deployed more soldiers to suppress the Leites than it had sent to fight Napoleon in Spain. The Leites lost. They were always going to lose, but they were not wrong that something was being taken from them. This is the paradox at the heart of the industrial revolution. Steam power did over the long term raise living standards for most people who lived under it. Real wages in Britain roughly doubled [music] between 1780 and 1850. Life expectancy after falling sharply in the new [music] industrial cities eventually began to climb. The brutal poverty of pre-industrial [music] agricultural England was replaced over time by something less brutal. But over time is doing a lot of work in that sentence. For the people alive during the first 50 years of steam, the benefits were unevenly distributed, and the costs were immediate and personal. The machine didn't care. It just kept running. What steam power actually changed at its deepest level wasn't manufacturing or transportation. Those were symptoms. What had changed was the human relationship with time and distance. Before steam, both of those things were fixed by biology and weather. A letter from London to Edinburgh moved at the speed of a horse and the condition of the road. News of a battle reached [music] a capital city days or weeks after the battle was over. A business decision made in Boston could take months to have any effect in Louisiana. The world was enormous in a way we no longer have the ability to feel. Steam compressed [music] it. Railroads compressed distance and the telegraph which followed the railroads because it needed the same right of way across the landscape compressed time. By 1866, a transatlantic telegraph cable connected Europe and North America. A message that had previously taken weeks to cross the ocean now took minutes. The world didn't just feel smaller, it actually was smaller in every way that mattered economically and politically. Steam also established a template that the next two centuries never stopped following. The pattern it demonstrated was [music] this. Find a dense concentrated energy source. Burn it to produce heat. Convert that heat into mechanical work. Burn more, do more. Scale up, extract more, burn more. Every coal fired power plant built in the 20th century runs on the same principle as Watts [music] engine. So does every nuclear power plant. The reactor is just a different way of making heat. The steam turbines that generate most of the world's electricity today are direct descendants of the engineering lineage that runs back through Stevenson to Watt to Newman to Savory. The carbon that is currently reshaping the planet's climate was put there by the same logic. Burn something to make steam. Make steam to make power. Make power to run the world. We are still inside the decision that was made in the minds of 18th [music] century England. The logic of it hasn't changed. Only the scale has. There is a particular kind of revolution that doesn't announce itself. It doesn't come with a single dramatic moment, a battle or a declaration, a clear before and after. It comes through a thousand small decisions, most of them made by people trying to solve an immediate practical problem, none of whom could see what they were actually building. Thomas Savory was trying to keep a mind from flooding. Thomas Newman was trying to do it better. James Watt [music] was trying to figure out why a small model wasn't working properly. Richard Trevoric was trying to find a use [music] for high pressure steam. George Stevenson was trying to win a railway contract. None of them set out to [music] change the world. They were just trying to solve the problem in front of them. And then one day, the [music] world they had quietly, incrementally remade, looked back at them and it was unrecognizable. We live inside that world now. Every time [music] you fill a kettle, every time you board a train, every time you turn on a light switch, you are at the end of a chain of consequences that began in the flooded coal mines of the 18th century England. Steam power didn't just change what humans could do. It changed [music] what humans thought was possible. And that second thing, the expansion of what seems possible, may be the most consequential thing any technology [music] has ever done. The water is boiling as it always has been, as it always will be. The question is what you build with it. If you made it this far, [music] I hope this story landed the way it was meant to. The history of how the modern world actually got built. [music] Not the myths of it, but the real story of the men, the machines, the breakthroughs, and the costs is something I genuinely believe everyone should understand. It explains more about how we live now than almost anything else. If that kind of history is what [music] you're after, subscribing is the best way to make sure you don't miss what's coming next. New stories go up regularly, and every one of them is built the same way this one was, starting with the question of what actually happened and following [music] it wherever it leads. Thanks for watching.
